passage:
In their Nairobi flat, Wanjiru's father held up the maths report. "Thirty-one percent? Thirty-one? What were you doing all term?" His voice filled the whole sitting room.
Wanjiru stared at the carpet. Her throat was tight, and she felt about as big as a bean. Anything she said now would come out wrong, so she said nothing.
Her father stomped out to the balcony.
After dinner, when the dishes were done and his face had softened, she brought him her maths book. "Baba, I want to do better. I don't understand fractions. Can we make a plan?"
He sat down slowly. "I shouted too much," he said. "Yes. Let's make one."
They wrote it together: half an hour every evening with him, and a study group with her classmate Bilal on Saturdays.

qa.q: What percentage did Wanjiru get in maths?
qa.a: Thirty-one percent.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru feel while her father shouted?
qa.a: Small and hurt, about as big as a bean, with a tight throat.

qa.q: Why was waiting until after dinner a wise choice?
qa.a: Her father had calmed down, so he could hear that she wanted to improve and help her make a plan.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru's father see things once he had cooled down?
qa.a: He admitted he had shouted too much and was ready to help her plan.

grounding: A girl goes quiet when her parent shouts about her failing marks, then waits until things cool and asks for help with a plan.

passage:
At the parent-teacher meeting, the class teacher showed Lalremsiami's mother the red marks on her science paper. In the corridor afterwards, her mother's voice rose so loudly that other parents turned. "Failing? After all the tuition? Do you even try?"
Lalremsiami's face went hot. She looked at her shoes. Her classmate Zubin, waiting with his father, looked away politely, which somehow made it worse. She felt tiny.
She didn't answer back. Anything she said would start a bigger fight.
In the school car park, her mother sat in the car and rubbed her forehead, quieter now. Lalremsiami took a breath. "Mama, I want to do better. The chapters on light confuse me. Can we ask Ma'am for extra worksheets and go through them together?"
Her mother looked at her for a long moment. "Yes. I'm sorry I shouted in there."

qa.q: Which chapters confuse Lalremsiami?
qa.a: The chapters on light.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling in the corridor?
qa.a: Embarrassed and tiny, with her face hot, made worse by Zubin being nearby.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do once things had cooled down?
qa.a: She said she wanted to improve and asked her mother to get extra worksheets and go through them together.

qa.q: How might her mother have felt sitting in the car rubbing her forehead?
qa.a: Worried and perhaps regretful about shouting in public; she then apologised.

grounding: A girl whose parent shouts about her failed test in public stays quiet, waits for calm and then asks for help with a plan.

passage:
The spelling test came back to Wanjiru with a big 4/20 in the corner. It was her second term in Oslo, and Norwegian words still tangled on her tongue. She folded the paper small.
When the bell rang, Ms. Ulla said, "Wanjiru, can you stay five minutes?" Wanjiru's stomach dropped.
But Ms. Ulla pulled a chair up beside her and unfolded the paper gently. "Look, most mistakes are the same kind: letters that sound different from English. That's normal. Let's make a little list of those, and I'll check it with you every Tuesday."
They worked until the cleaner came in. Walking to the bus, Wanjiru realised she wasn't embarrassed any more. Ms. Ulla had stayed because she thought Wanjiru could do it.

qa.q: What score did Wanjiru get in the spelling test?
How did Wanjiru feel walking to the bus?
qa.a: No longer embarrassed; she felt cared for and believed in.

qa.q: What made Ms. Ulla's help effective?
qa.a: She found the pattern in the mistakes, made a small list and set regular Tuesday checks.

qa.q: How does Ms. Ulla see Wanjiru's low score?
qa.a: As a normal stage in learning a new language, not a sign that Wanjiru cannot do it.

grounding: A girl whose teacher stays back to explain her mistakes feels cared for and sees that accepting help means someone believes she can improve.

passage:
The staff room was empty except for Irawati Ma'am and a pile of notebooks. She had asked Bidisha to come after school with her failed geometry paper.
Bidisha dragged her feet. Only the weak kids got called for extra help, she thought. What if someone saw?
Irawati Ma'am cleared a space. "Show me number six. Tell me what you were thinking." Bidisha explained, stumbling. Ma'am nodded. "Your thinking was right until here. You forgot that angles on a straight line add up to 180. That's all."
They did three more together. On the third, Bidisha got it before Ma'am spoke.
"You see?" Ma'am smiled. "I don't stay back for students I've given up on."
Bidisha walked out warm-faced, but not from embarrassment.

qa.q: Which question did Irawati Ma'am ask to see first?
qa.a: Number six.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha drag her feet to the staff room?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, thinking only weak students got extra help, and worried someone would see.

qa.q: How did Irawati Ma'am help Bidisha learn from the mistake?
qa.a: She asked Bidisha to explain her thinking, pinpointed the one forgotten rule and practised three more with her.

qa.q: What does staying back mean to Irawati Ma'am?
qa.a: It shows she believes the student can improve; she does not stay back for students she has given up on.

grounding: A girl ashamed to need extra help finds her teacher's time after school means the teacher believes she can improve.

passage: Kashish, that boy laughed at your marks? Come, sit on the swing with your Mridul Dadu. When I was your age, I got four out of twenty-five in a geography test. Bhola, the loudest boy in class, grabbed my paper and waved it. "Four! Even my buffalo would get five!" Everyone laughed. My ears burned. I wanted to hit him. Instead I said, "Maybe your buffalo should sit the next test," took my paper back and walked off. Some boys laughed at him then. Later that year I found Bhola crying behind the school because he couldn't read the long words in the Hindi book. I could. So I helped him, and he helped me with maps. You see, beta, one score is just one day. And the one who laughs has weak spots too.

qa.q: What did Bhola say his buffalo would get?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: How did young Mridul feel when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Humiliated and angry; his ears burned and he wanted to hit Bhola.

qa.q: What choice in Dadu's story worked better than hitting Bhola?
qa.a: Answering calmly with a joke, taking the paper back and walking away.

qa.q: What was Bhola hiding behind his loud laughing?
qa.a: His own struggle with reading, which he cried about behind the school.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a classmate mocking his low marks, answering calmly and later seeing that the mocker had weak spots too.

passage:
The half-yearly results were pinned on the noticeboard, and the whole of Class 6 crowded round it before the last bus. Joseph found his name: Maths, 28 out of 80. Red ink.
"Twenty-eight!" Pankaj crowed, loud enough for everyone. "Joseph, did you write with your eyes shut?"
A few kids snorted. Joseph's stomach dropped and his face went hot. The bus horn honked outside; he had maybe one minute.
He thought of a hundred nasty replies. Pankaj couldn't swim a single length in PE; everyone knew. But he didn't say it.
"One test, Pankaj," he said evenly. "I'll do better next time." Then he picked up his bag and walked out to the bus.
On the ride home his heart slowed. Pankaj's words had hurt, but they hadn't changed who he was.

qa.q: What did Joseph score in maths?
qa.a: 28 out of 80.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Pankaj crowed?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed; his stomach dropped and his face went hot.

qa.q: What did Joseph choose instead of a nasty reply?
qa.a: He answered calmly that it was one test and walked out to the bus.

qa.q: What would change if Joseph had mentioned Pankaj's swimming?
qa.a: It could have turned into a public fight and hurt Pankaj too, instead of ending the mockery.

grounding: A boy mocked for his marks answers calmly and walks away, knowing one score does not define him and that the mocker has weak spots too.

passage:
Sonali sat on the steps of the village temple with her failed English paper in her lap. Seventeen out of fifty. The goats nibbled the grass below, not interested.
Lalit, her friend from the next farm, sat down beside her and glanced at the paper. "Seventeen? I got nineteen last year. I cried in the cowshed."
Sonali looked up. "You? You're good at everything."
"Not English. Tenses make my head spin. Want to do it together? Master-ji said we can use the panchayat library after four."
For the next month they sat at the library's wobbly table every evening, testing each other from a torn grammar book. When Sonali got a sentence right, Lalit clapped. When he forgot, she corrected him.
In the next test Sonali got thirty-four. Lalit got thirty-six. They bought one orange ice lolly and shared it.

qa.q: What did Sonali get in her English paper?
qa.a: Seventeen out of fifty.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when Lalit said he had also struggled?
qa.a: Surprised and less alone, since she had thought he was good at everything.

qa.q: How did studying together turn the failure around?
qa.a: They tested each other every evening at the library, making her failure a shared problem with a plan, and both improved.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel helping Sonali?
qa.a: Glad and understanding, since he remembered crying over his own low marks.

grounding: A girl who failed a test is comforted when a friend says he struggled too and offers to study together.

passage:
Amara pushed her history test into her locker so hard the door bounced back. Five out of twenty. Her family had only been in Madrid a year, and all the dates and kings swam together.
Diego leaned on the next locker. "Bad?"
She nodded, not trusting her voice.
"Last year I failed maths twice," he said. "My mum cried more than I did. Then my cousin made me flashcards, and it got better." He shrugged. "Want to do history flashcards? I'm terrible at dates too."
That afternoon they sat at the back table of his aunt's cafe, making cards with drawings: a king with a crown of oranges, a ship made of numbers. They quizzed each other over hot chocolate.
Amara walked home feeling lighter. The failure hadn't vanished, but it had become a project for two.

qa.q: What score did Amara get in the history test?
qa.a: Five out of twenty.

qa.q: How did Amara feel after the afternoon at the cafe?
qa.a: Lighter and less alone, since the failure had become a shared project.

qa.q: What made Diego's offer so helpful?
qa.a: He admitted his own failures and offered a concrete plan: making flashcards together.

qa.q: How might Diego see Amara's failed test?
qa.a: As something he understands from failing maths twice himself, not something to judge.

grounding: A girl upset about a failed test is helped by a friend who admits he struggled too and offers to study with her.

passage:
After failing the decimals test, Tanuja drew a chart on the back of an old calendar and pinned it above her bed in their small house in Hoshangabad. Thirty boxes, one for each day. Rule: ten decimal sums every evening, before anything else.
The first week was awful. She got six wrong on Monday and wanted to rip the chart down. "I'm so stupid," she muttered.
Her brother Mridul, doing his own homework on the floor, said, "You got four right. Last week you got zero."
Tanuja stopped. That was true. She coloured Monday's box yellow anyway.
By the third week most boxes were green. On the twentieth day she got all ten right and did a silly dance on the bed. The chart stayed up, yellow Monday and all.

qa.q: How many decimal sums did Tanuja do every evening?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling on the first Monday?
qa.a: Frustrated and discouraged; she called herself stupid and wanted to rip the chart down.

qa.q: How did Mridul's comment help Tanuja keep going?
qa.a: He pointed out she had gone from zero to four right, helping her notice progress instead of hating herself.

qa.q: How might Mridul see Tanuja's chart by the third week?
qa.a: Probably impressed and proud of his sister's steady effort.

grounding: After failing, a girl practises the hard chapter every day, learns to look at mistakes without hating herself and celebrates small improvements.

passage:
Mateo got his science test back in Lima with a 9 out of 20, and every mistake was on the water cycle. On the bus home he felt hot and stupid. Then he stopped himself. Stupid people didn't get the other chapters right, and he had.
That night he made a deal with himself: draw the water cycle once a day for two weeks, without looking.
Day one was a mess; he forgot where clouds come from. On day four he remembered evaporation. His friend Amara saw the drawings on his desk. "Your clouds look like sheep," she laughed, but she quizzed him too.
On day eleven he drew the whole cycle perfectly and stuck it on the fridge with a star. His mother added a second star beside it.

qa.q: What score did Mateo get in the science test?
qa.a: 9 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Mateo stop himself from feeling stupid?
qa.a: He felt hot and stupid at first, then reminded himself that he had got the other chapters right.

qa.q: What plan did Mateo make, and how did he mark his progress?
qa.a: To draw the water cycle once a day for two weeks without looking; he celebrated with a star on the fridge.

qa.q: How might Mateo's mother see the drawing on the fridge?
qa.a: As proof of his steady effort, so she proudly added a second star.

grounding: After failing, a boy decides to practise the hard topic every day, treats his mistakes without self-hatred and celebrates improvement.

passage:
In Ammachi's old house near Kottayam, the power went off every night at ten, and the coconut palms threw long, waving shadows across Thomas's room. In the corner, the hanging umbrella looked exactly like a tall man in a hat. Thomas pulled the sheet over his head and held his breath.
"Are you awake?" whispered his cousin Hrithik from the other bed. "That umbrella looks like a ghost."
"You're scared too?"
"Obviously."
In the morning they told Ammachi. She didn't laugh. She moved the umbrella to the veranda and gave them a small battery lamp to keep on low all night. "Fear is real even when the ghost is not," she said.
That night the shadows still moved. But with the little light on, Thomas could see they were only leaves.

qa.q: What did the hanging umbrella look like to Thomas?
qa.a: A tall man in a hat.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when Hrithik admitted being scared too?
qa.a: Relieved and less alone, since the fear was shared.

qa.q: What helped the boys with their fear of the dark?
qa.a: Telling Ammachi, moving the umbrella and keeping a small battery lamp on low.

qa.q: How does Ammachi see the boys' fear?
qa.a: As real even though the ghost is not; she takes it seriously instead of laughing.

grounding: A boy scared of the dark imagines shapes in the corner; talking about it and a small light help the fear fade.

passage:
It was Zeynep's first sleepover, at Wei's flat in Berlin. When Wei's mother switched off the light, the room went completely black. Zeynep's heart began to thud. The wardrobe door was open a crack. What if something was inside?
She lay stiff for ten minutes. Then she whispered, "Wei? I'm scared of the dark. At home I have a little light."
There was a pause. "I used to be scared of the wardrobe," Wei whispered back. "Mama! Can we have the moon lamp?"
Wei's mother came in with a small lamp shaped like a moon and set it on the shelf. She also shut the wardrobe door firmly. "There. Only jumpers in there."
In the soft glow, Zeynep could see it was only a room. They talked about school until they fell asleep.

qa.q: What shape was the small lamp?
qa.a: Like a moon.

qa.q: What was Zeynep afraid of when the light went off?
qa.a: She was scared something might be inside the wardrobe; her heart was thudding.

qa.q: What helped Zeynep feel safe?
qa.a: Saying she was scared, a small light, and Wei's mother shutting the wardrobe.

qa.q: How did Wei respond to Zeynep's fear?
qa.a: Wei understood, having once feared the wardrobe too, and asked for the moon lamp.

grounding: A girl scared of the dark at a sleepover talks about it, and a small light helps the imagined danger fade.

passage:
Thunder cracked right over the house at two in the morning, and Damini woke screaming from a dream about falling down a well. The power was out and the fan had stopped. Everything was black and loud.
"Mumma!"
Mumma had an early shift at the hospital in four hours, but she came at once with a candle. She sat on the edge of the bed and put Damini's hand on her own chest. "Feel that? Slow and steady. You're safe. It was a dream. I'm right here."
Damini's breaths were short and fast at first. Mumma breathed slowly, in and out, and Damini copied. Thud, thud. Slower.
"Will you stay?"
"Till you sleep."
Her little sister Aditi crept in too and curled up at the foot of the bed. By the next thunderclap, Damini was barely awake.

qa.q: What did Damini dream about?
qa.a: Falling down a well.

qa.q: How did Damini feel when she woke in the storm?
qa.a: Terrified; she screamed, and her breaths were short and fast.

qa.q: What did Mumma do that calmed Damini?
qa.a: She came at once, said Damini was safe, and helped her copy slow breathing with a hand on Mumma's chest.

qa.q: How might Mumma have felt with an early shift only four hours away?
qa.a: Tired, but she chose to comfort Damini straight away and stay until she slept.

grounding: A girl woken by a nightmare in a storm is calmed by her mother sitting beside her and saying she is safe.

passage:
In their flat in Hyderabad, Madhuri woke sweating. In the dream she had been lost in a crowded market, calling for Amma, and nobody turned around. Her heart was galloping.
She padded into the next room. Amma lifted her head from the pillow, then pulled back the sheet without a word. Madhuri crawled in.
"Bad dream?" Amma whispered.
Madhuri nodded, then told her the whole thing: the market, the calling, the faces that didn't turn.
Amma stroked her hair. "You're here, in your own home. I can hear you. I will always turn around."
Saying it out loud made the dream look smaller, like a paper boat instead of a ship. Her heart slowed to match Amma's breathing.
In the morning her little brother Pradeep asked why she was in Amma's bed. "Sharing a dream," Madhuri said, "makes it shrink."

qa.q: Where was Madhuri lost in her dream?
qa.a: In a crowded market.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel when she woke?
qa.a: Frightened, sweating, with a galloping heart.

qa.q: What made the dream feel smaller?
qa.a: Telling Amma the whole dream out loud while Amma reassured her.

qa.q: How does Amma respond to Madhuri's fear?
qa.a: Calmly and warmly, making room without questions first and promising she will always turn around.

grounding: A girl frightened by a nightmare shares it with her mother, whose calm reassurance makes the fear smaller.

passage:
Swimming coach's note, Saturday
Manoj was not ready to jump from the high board today and stood at the edge a long time before climbing down. His friend Ayesha called out from the water, "Scaredy-cat Manoj!" and a few children laughed. I saw his jaw tighten.
Before I could step in, he answered calmly, "Everyone's scared of something. What about you and lizards?" Ayesha went pink and giggled, and the laughter turned to lizards instead.
I told Manoj he could take the boards step by step, starting from the low one, and that nobody on my team needs to prove anything by rushing. I also had a quiet word with Ayesha about teasing. At the end of practice, Manoj jumped from the low board twice, grinning.

qa.q: Where did Manoj jump from at the end of practice?
qa.a: The low board, twice.

qa.q: What did Manoj's tightened jaw suggest?
qa.a: He felt stung and embarrassed by the teasing.

qa.q: How did Manoj handle Ayesha's teasing?
qa.a: He calmly said everyone is scared of something and pointed to her own fear of lizards.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when Manoj mentioned lizards?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a bit caught out, realising she has fears too.

grounding: A coach's note shows a boy teased as a scaredy-cat by a friend, who answers that everyone is afraid of something.

passage:
Sunday
At the fair today, Dhruv wanted everyone to go into the Ghost Tunnel. I said no. I could hear the screaming from outside, and my legs felt like jelly.
"Scaredy-cat Sharmila!" he sang, and made chicken noises. The others laughed. That stung, a lot.
I nearly went in just to shut him up. But I didn't want to. So I said, "Everyone's scared of something, Dhruv. You wouldn't even touch the snake at the science fair."
He stopped clucking.
Mehr and I went on the giant wheel instead and saw the whole town lit up. Mehr didn't tease me once. I think I'll sit with Mehr more.
Sharmila

qa.q: Which ride did Dhruv want everyone to go on?
qa.a: The Ghost Tunnel.

qa.q: How did Dhruv's teasing make Sharmila feel?
qa.a: It stung a lot, and Sharmila felt pushed to go in just to shut him up.

qa.q: What did Sharmila choose instead of proving bravery?
qa.a: To say everyone is scared of something, then enjoy the giant wheel with Mehr, a friend who does not tease.

qa.q: Why might Dhruv have stopped clucking?
qa.a: Being reminded of his own fear of the snake showed him he was not so fearless either.

grounding: A child teased as a scaredy-cat says everyone is afraid of something and chooses a friend who does not tease.

passage:
Gautam had to recite his poem at the school annual day, and ten minutes before his turn the microphone died. The teacher whispered, "You'll have to speak loudly without it." His knees shook. Three hundred parents sat out there.
He walked on anyway, took a breath, and said the first line too softly. Then he thought of Dadi in the back row and said the rest loud and clear. The clapping felt like rain on a hot day.
Afterwards his friend Saurabh slapped his back. "Brave! Now jump off the stage wall like a real hero. It's only two metres."
Gautam looked at the drop and laughed. "No thanks. I've done my brave thing for today."
He walked down the steps instead, still glowing.

qa.q: What happened ten minutes before Gautam's turn?
qa.a: The microphone died.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel after the poem?
qa.a: Proud and glowing; the clapping felt like rain on a hot day.

qa.q: Why was saying no to the wall jump a wise choice?
qa.a: He had already faced his real fear; jumping would risk injury just to prove bravery.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Gautam's refusal?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised, but he may realise Gautam had already shown real bravery on stage.

grounding: A boy faces his fear of speaking on stage, feels proud, and refuses to prove bravery by risking his safety.

passage:
At the municipal pool in Nagpur, Bhupen had stayed in the shallow end for six weeks. Today Coach said he was ready to swim one full length, all the way to the deep end.
He stood at the edge, stomach flipping. Reena, from his batch, called out, "Just go! If you get scared, grab the rope!"
He pushed off. Halfway, the floor dropped away below him and panic prickled up his arms. He kept kicking, counting strokes, and his hand smacked the far wall.
He'd done it! He clung there, laughing and spluttering. Coach gave a thumbs-up.
Later Reena said, "Now try the high board!" Bhupen shook his head. "Coach says not till next month. One scary thing a day is enough." He floated on his back, feeling ten feet tall.

qa.q: How long had Bhupen stayed in the shallow end?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel when he touched the far wall?
qa.a: Proud and happy, laughing and feeling ten feet tall.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen say no to the high board?
qa.a: Coach had said not until next month, and he did not need to prove bravery by rushing into risk.

qa.q: How might Reena see Bhupen's swim?
qa.a: She cheered him on and was probably happy for him, even suggesting the next challenge.

grounding: A boy faces his fear of deep water, feels proud, and declines to prove more bravery by taking a risk before he is ready.

passage:
On the school bus in Cape Town, a big boy from Grade 7 slid into the seat next to Lindiwe and leaned close. "Bring me ten rand every day, or you'll be sorry after school." He cracked his knuckles.
Lindiwe's whole body went cold. She nodded without meaning to. All morning she couldn't hear a word in class.
At break her friend Hiroshi found her hiding by the library. "You look sick. What's wrong?"
She told him, shaking. "If I tell, he'll get me."
"That's exactly why you have to tell. I'll come with you."
They went straight to Mrs. Petersen. She listened and said, "You were right to tell me. This is not your fault." Before the last bell she had spoken to the boy and the principal, phoned Lindiwe's mother, and arranged for a teacher to ride the bus that afternoon.

qa.q: What did the boy tell Lindiwe to bring every day?
qa.a: Ten rand.

qa.q: How did Lindiwe feel after the boy threatened her?
qa.a: Terrified; her whole body went cold and she could not hear a word in class.

qa.q: What did Mrs. Petersen do the same day?
qa.a: She reassured Lindiwe, spoke to the boy and the principal, phoned her mother and arranged for a teacher to ride the bus.

qa.q: How did Hiroshi see Lindiwe's fear of telling?
qa.a: He understood it but believed telling was exactly what was needed, so he went with her.

grounding: A girl terrified by an older boy's threats tells a teacher with a friend's support, and the teacher acts the same day.

passage:
At the sports hostel, a Class 9 boy blocked Deepak's way outside the shower room. "You tell Coach I pushed you on court, and your racket's finished. Understand?" He shoved Deepak against the wall and walked off.
Deepak's hands shook so badly he dropped his soap. At dinner he couldn't eat. He kept watching the door.
Aparna, the senior girl who ran study hour, noticed. "Deepak, what's going on? You look scared stiff."
"Nothing." Then, very quietly: "If I tell, he'll get me."
"Telling isn't weak. It's smart. And you won't be alone. Come."
She walked him straight to the warden's office. The warden listened to all of it, said, "Thank you for telling me. You did nothing wrong," called the coach, and moved Deepak to the room next to the warden's that same night. The older boy was spoken to before lights-out.

qa.q: What did the older boy threaten about Deepak's racket?
qa.a: That it would be finished if Deepak told Coach.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel at dinner?
qa.a: Terrified; he could not eat and kept watching the door.

qa.q: What did the warden do that night?
qa.a: Listened, reassured Deepak, called the coach, moved him next to the warden's room and had the older boy spoken to before lights-out.

qa.q: How did Aparna see Deepak's fear?
qa.a: She noticed he looked scared stiff and saw telling as smart, not weak, so she took him to the warden.

grounding: A boy terrified by an older boy's threat is helped to tell a trusted adult, who acts that same night.
